headline: High: shared filesystem plus AutoGPT shell/network access and OpenMetadata MCP/webhooks create dangerous default pathways for leakage, conflict, and cascading errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: AutoGPT can read and act on filesystem content and execute shell commands, while OpenMetadata exposes MCP tools, APIs, events, and webhooks. That creates a plausible instruction-injection bridge if OpenMetadata content is surfaced into AutoGPT without filtering. The pairwise pathway is inferred, not directly documented, so uncertainty pushes above low.
conditions: IF OpenMetadata content is copied into AutoGPT prompts or files without provenance filtering
IF AutoGPT is allowed to execute shell commands on content originating from OpenMetadata webhooks or MCP outputs
mitigations: Disable automatic ingestion of OpenMetadata outputs into AutoGPT prompts
Add a provenance tag to all OpenMetadata-derived text before AutoGPT reads it
Restrict AutoGPT shell execution to a dry-run mode for untrusted inputs
requires-engineering: insert a sanitizer between OpenMetadata webhooks and AutoGPT
requires-engineering: isolate the two agents on separate workspaces

B_data_leakage.rationale: AutoGPT has filesystem access and allowlisted network egress, while OpenMetadata handles governance, lineage, and memory/trust metadata through APIs, SDKs, events, webhooks, and MCP. If they share a workspace, sensitive catalog data can flow from files into AutoGPT’s outbound requests. The profiles do not prove a shared workspace by default, so this remains medium rather than high.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same filesystem or mounted workspace
IF OpenMetadata data classes are written to files that AutoGPT can read
IF AutoGPT is permitted to send file-derived context to external APIs
mitigations: Separate the agents onto different workspaces
Block AutoGPT from reading OpenMetadata export directories
Limit AutoGPT egress to a test endpoint during shared runs
requires-engineering: encrypt or redact catalog exports before sharing
requires-engineering: add DLP checks on outbound AutoGPT requests

C_capability_conflict.rationale: AutoGPT can execute shell commands and spawn subprocesses, and OpenMetadata can run multiple instances and interact through APIs, events, webhooks, and MCP. If both touch the same mutable files or deployment state, concurrent writes can collide. The profiles do not show locking or shared-write guarantees, so the conflict is plausible in default deployments but not proven high.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory, database, or git checkout
IF OpenMetadata events trigger AutoGPT actions against the same mutable resource
IF no external lock or transaction boundary is configured
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate writable directory
Disable concurrent writes to shared resources
Use a lock file or lease before either agent mutates state
requires-engineering: route writes through a single coordinator
requires-engineering: add optimistic-concurrency checks on shared resources

D_cascading_error.rationale: OpenMetadata’s APIs, events, webhooks, and MCP outputs can become inputs to AutoGPT, which can then execute shell commands and subprocesses. That is a classic unverified-output-to-action chain. Because AutoGPT can take real actions and OpenMetadata can emit operational signals, a bad catalog fact can cascade into destructive automation unless explicitly verified.
conditions: IF AutoGPT treats OpenMetadata outputs as authoritative without a verification step
IF OpenMetadata webhooks or MCP responses are used to trigger AutoGPT actions
IF AutoGPT is allowed to execute commands based on those outputs
mitigations: Require human approval before AutoGPT acts on OpenMetadata-derived facts
Add a verification step against the source system before execution
Restrict AutoGPT to read-only mode for OpenMetadata-fed tasks
requires-engineering: implement schema validation for all OpenMetadata inputs
requires-engineering: add rollback or dry-run wrappers around AutoGPT actions

E_compliance.rationale: OpenMetadata explicitly touches governance, lineage, and memory/trust metadata, while AutoGPT can read files and send data over allowlisted egress. If regulated metadata or personal data is stored in the shared workspace, residency or retention mismatches can arise. The profiles do not specify HIPAA/GDPR/DPA terms, so I cannot justify high severity; uncertainty keeps this at medium.
conditions: IF regulated or personal data is present in OpenMetadata-managed records
IF AutoGPT exports that data to a third-party endpoint outside the required residency boundary
IF retention or deletion policies differ between the two systems
mitigations: Classify the data before sharing it with AutoGPT
Block export of regulated fields from OpenMetadata to AutoGPT
Review retention settings on both systems
requires-engineering: enforce residency-aware routing for outbound requests
requires-engineering: add deletion/export workflows across both systems
